title: Categorical Tensor-Graph Semantics for Quantum Algorithms
authors: Naihong Hu, Ruining Li, Futao Wang
abstract: This paper systematically investigates quantum computing protocols from the intuitive perspective of categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb. While conventional Hilbert-space formalisms conceal the structural nature of quantum algorithms behind high-dimensional matrix operations, the topological framework developed herein directly encodes algorithmic functionalities to their graphical skeletons. We provide a comprehensive topological reinterpretation of the Bernstein-Vazirani and the Simon algorithms, demonstrating how topological transformations distill their core mathematical essence and clarify the operational mechanism of oracles. Going beyond standard qubit models, we formalize the qutrit-adapted generalized Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm as well as the generalized single-shot Grover algorithm, explicitly laying out their graphical representations. We further implement CNOT gates via complementary Frobenius structures, trace the diagrammatic genesis of quantum entanglement including Bell and GHZ states, and present a diagrammatic simplification for W-state preparation protocol. By bridging tensor category theory with practical quantum algorithmic design, this work furnishes composable, scalable diagrammatic toolkit essential for automated circuit optimization across the evolving quantum hardware ecosystem.
summary: This paper develops a novel framework using categorical tensor-graph semantics to analyze quantum algorithms structurally. It reinterprets key protocols like Bernstein-Vazirani and generalizes them to higher dimensions (qutrits) within this topological language. By linking computation to Frobenius structures, it provides a powerful diagrammatic toolkit for circuit optimization and understanding entanglement.
main_problem: To provide a structural, intuitive understanding of quantum algorithms by reinterpreting them using categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb.
main_result: The paper establishes that fundamental quantum operations like entanglement generation and algorithm execution can be mapped to algebraic structures (Frobenius structures) whose properties reveal deep mathematical connections between computation and topology.
method: It employs advanced tools from category theory, specifically utilizing tensor-graph semantics and Frobenius structures, to topologically reinterpret established quantum algorithms and physical processes.
model_or_system: The focus is on abstract quantum computation within finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces (FHilb), analyzing protocols involving qubits and qutrits. The formalism uses monoidal dagger categories to define state preparation and gate operations diagrammatically.
key_observables: Topological skeletons of algorithms, entanglement properties (non-copyability), and the structure constants derived from complementary Frobenius structures.
important_parameters: The dimension of the Hilbert space ($n$), the base field ($\mathbb{C}_2$ for some analyses), and the constant $s$ characterizing complementary bases.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that complex quantum operations can be accurately modeled and understood through the lens of categorical algebraic structures like Frobenius algebras.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate tensor diagrams for algorithms (BV, Simon) and state preparation protocols (Bell, GHZ, W-state), alongside formal definitions for various categorical structures (monoid, comonoid, Frobenius structure).
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the necessary algebraic framework (Frobenius structures in FHilb) to applying this framework to reinterpret specific quantum algorithms (BV, Simon, Deutsch-Jozsa generalization), and finally analyzing physical phenomena like entanglement using these structural tools.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, the development of a diagrammatic toolkit based on category theory offers a powerful, potentially automated way to optimize quantum circuits by revealing underlying mathematical symmetries beyond standard gate decomposition.
